newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand fragile but moving positively-Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Thailand fragile but moving positively-Merrill.

text.p: Thailand's economic fundamentals are still fragile but they are moving in a positive direction despite turmoil in the troubled finance sector, Merrill Lynch said in its latest report on Monday.
Although there were concerns over rising non-performing loans in the banking sector, the financial institutions would be able to weather any rough times in the future.

"Although banks are suffering from NPL (non-performing loan) problems, their threshold of pain is high because risks have been appropriately priced, as reflected in their high ROE of 21 percent and gross spreads of over 400 baht per share," Merrill said in the report.
"We think the probability of a vicious trap involving a banking crisis and a GDP slump (in a manner of Japan) is low as Thai banks have priced loan risks appropriately in the past," it said.
A slowdown in the Thai economy and increasing poor quality assets as a result of high exposure to depressed property sector raised concerns over the soundness of the finance sector, analysts said.
In a sweeping revamp of the sector, Thai authorities last week ordered finance firms and banks to raise provisions on poor quality loans.
They also told 10 weakened finance companies to boost capital by 8.25 billion baht ($317 million)
Markets tumbled last week as rumours of the poor health of some firms in the finance sector, previously denied by the authorities, were brought to light.
But Merrill Lynch maintained that any negative impact on commercial banks will be limited.

"Our simulation suggests that even with a jump in NPL to 17-18 percent, banks can be self-capitalising at a loan growth rate of 11 percent...Therefore, it is unlikely that banking problems would be a major drag on the economy as in Japan," it said in the report.

Merrill said Thailand's macroeconomic perspective was more optimistic than the microeconomic side, with cyclical improvement just starting and recently sluggish exports seen becoming more bullish this year.
"With the U.S. economy hitting full capacity, we believe its elasticity to import is very high," the report said.

"Coupled with a rising electronics cycle, better agricultural prices and a recovery in textile trade, Thai exports could turn out to be much stronger than the government's forecast of 10 percent for 1997," it said.
In 1996, Thai exports contracted by 0.2 percent versus nearly 24 percent growth posted in 1995.

However, it said several developments needed close monitoring and these included management of the economy, the nearly 100 billion baht of spending cuts for fiscal 1996/97 (September-October) announced by the government in February and political reform.

Although all political parties have expressed support for constitutional reform, aimed at refining Thailand's fledgling democracy, there were disagreements over specific changes to be made and this needed to be resolved.
Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh has vowed to push for political reform and to dissolve his six-party coalition government when the reforms are finalised.
